docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
Title: Introduction to American Sign Language (ASL): Communication Through Movement and Expression

Summary: This 6-week introductory ASL elective invites students in grades 4–8 to explore American Sign Language through games, movement, and creative activities. Each one-hour session introduces new vocabulary, signing techniques, and elements of Deaf culture in a fun, interactive environment designed for all learners—including those with dyslexia, ADHD, and related learning differences. The class emphasizes visual learning, communication, and self-expression through signing, without formal homework or assessments.

Intended Audience: Students in grades 4–8 who are curious about language, communication, and visual expression. This class welcomes beginners and encourages participation from students who enjoy hands-on, movement-based learning and peer interaction.

Prerequisites:

  • No prior ASL experience required.
  • Students should be comfortable participating in small group games and interactive activities.
  • A willingness to use facial expressions and body language as part of communication.

docs.title: Remember (Recall facts and basic concepts)
docs.text:
Students will be able to:

  • Recognize and recall ASL letters, numbers, and key vocabulary.
  • Identify basic conversational signs such as greetings, feelings, and family terms.
  • Recall etiquette and key facts about Deaf culture and communication norms.

docs.title: Understand (Explain ideas or concepts)
docs.text:
Students will be able to:

  • Explain the importance of facial expression and body language in ASL.
  • Describe how ASL differs from English and why it is a complete language.
  • Summarize ways Deaf and hearing communities communicate effectively.

docs.title: Apply (Use information in new situations)
docs.text:
Students will be able to:

  • Use ASL signs in short, real-life interactions (introductions, feelings, favorites).
  • Demonstrate ASL communication through skits, games, and partner activities.
  • Participate in group storytelling or expressive signing activities.

docs.title: Analyze (Draw connections among ideas)
docs.text:
Students will be able to:

  • Compare spoken and signed communication.
  • Observe how visual-spatial language supports understanding and inclusion.
  • Recognize patterns in handshapes and movement that form categories of meaning.

docs.title: Evaluate (Justify a decision or course of action)
docs.text:
Students will be able to:

  • Reflect on the importance of accessible communication and inclusion.
  • Discuss how learning ASL can help bridge communication differences.

docs.title: Create (Produce original work)
docs.text:
Students will be able to:

  • Design and perform short ASL skits combining learned vocabulary.
  • Invent new ways to communicate emotions or ideas through sign.
  • Demonstrate expressive storytelling using signs, gestures, and facial expressions.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
Foundational Concepts: ASL alphabet and fingerspelling, greetings, conversational basics, Deaf culture awareness. Core Concepts: Emotions and feelings, family and people, food and favorites, animals and nature, colors and descriptions. Extended Concepts: Expressive storytelling, skits, and signed dialogue.

Concepts Explicitly Excluded:

  • Advanced ASL grammar or sentence structure.
  • Formal assessment or graded performance.
  • Interpretation or translation between ASL and English.

docs.title: Sample Class Activities (By Week)
docs.text:
• Week 1: Silent Name Game & Fingerspelling Challenge
  • Week 2: Emotion Charades – signing how you feel
  • Week 3: Build-a-Family signing game
  • Week 4: ASL Café – ordering and signing favorite foods
  • Week 5: Animal Charades and storytelling
  • Week 6: Mini Showcase – perform a short ASL skit using learned signs

docs.title: Optional Projects / Culminating Activities
docs.text:
Project Name: “My ASL Story” Description: Students create and perform a short, signed story using their favorite vocabulary. Skills Demonstrated: Visual communication, expressive signing, vocabulary application. Deliverable: Live performance or short recorded video of signed storytelling.

Project Name: “ASL in Action” Description: Students teach a friend or family member 5–10 ASL signs they’ve learned. Skills Demonstrated: Recall, explanation, and expressive use of ASL. Deliverable: Informal reflection or group share.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 12 chapters covering 200 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Introduction and ASL Foundations - Introduces the basic parameters of American Sign Language (handshape, palm orientation, location, movement, expression) and Deaf culture basics.
  2. Fingerspelling and Numbers - Teaches fingerspelling the ASL alphabet, numbers 1-100, counting techniques, and basic time and age expressions.
  3. Basic Conversational Phrases - Covers essential signs for greetings, politeness, simple questions, and basic everyday dialogue.
  4. Pronouns and Signing Space - Explores how to use personal pronouns, indexing, directionality, and the physical signing space to structure communication.
  5. Expressing Emotions and Feelings - Enables students to communicate different feelings, emotions, states of being, and varying degrees of emotional intensity.
  6. Family and People - Introduces signs for family members, friends, relationships, and different roles in school and the community.
  7. Food and Favorite Things - Focuses on food vocabulary, expressing likes/dislikes, ordering meals, and describing preferences.
  8. Animals and Nature - Covers signs for pets, common wild animals, plants, weather, and the natural environment.
  9. Describing the World - Introduces descriptive words including colors, size, speed, temperature, and general qualities.
  10. Action Verbs and Activities - Teaches common action signs for play, sports, school work, daily routines, and performances.
  11. ASL Grammar and Expression - Explores grammatical structures like role shifts, classifiers, agreement verbs, and non-manual signals (facial grammar).
  12. Deaf Culture and Communication - Examines Deaf identity, history, communication accessibility, regional sign variations, and visual storytelling.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
This textbook uses a step-by-step learning progression. Each chapter builds upon the concepts introduced in the previous chapters, ensuring that all prerequisites are met before advanced topics are introduced. We recommend completing the chapters in sequence.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

!!! mascot-welcome "Hi! I'm Mimi." { class="mascot-admonition-img" } Welcome to the ASL textbook! I'm Mimi, your friendly chameleon learning guide. Chameleons are famous for how they change colors to express themselves, which makes me the perfect helper for exploring American Sign Language—a language where visual expressions and hand movements are everything! I'll be popping up in the margins all the way through this book, but I don't show up randomly. I have exactly six jobs, and you'll learn to recognize what to do by the pose I'm in:

1. **Welcome you** at the start of every chapter — that's what I'm doing right now.
2. **Help you think things through** when a signing concept or cultural practice calls for extra reflection.
3. **Give you tips** — the helpful hints, tricks, and muscle-memory secrets that experienced signers use.
4. **Warn you gently** about common signing mistakes, cultural pitfalls, or fingerspelling traps.
5. **Encourage you** when a new handshape or physical movement feels tricky or unfamiliar.
6. **Celebrate with you** at the end of each chapter when you've mastered the concepts and earned your milestone.

That's it. If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Let's start our signing adventure together!

docs.title: 1. Understanding Communication Modes
docs.text: When we think of language, we often think of speaking and listening. However, human language is much broader. Communication can be divided into different channels, or modes, depending on how information is sent and received. Understanding these modes helps us see how American Sign Language is structured.

docs.title: Visual Communication vs. Auditory-Oral Communication
docs.text:
For hearing individuals, the primary mode of language is Auditory-Oral Communication. This system uses sound waves produced by the mouth (oral) and received by the ears (auditory). In contrast, Visual Communication relies on sight. It is a broad category that includes anything we see to gain information—from traffic signs and drawings to written words and body language.

American Sign Language (ASL) operates entirely within the visual mode. Instead of sound, it uses a Visual-Gestural channel. The signer produces messages using body movement, hands, and facial expressions, and the receiver processes this information through their eyes.

docs.title: Manual Communication
docs.text:
Within visual communication, we find Manual Communication. This refers specifically to using the hands, arms, and body to transmit messages. Manual communication has a long history, appearing in gestural systems, historical monastic sign codes, and modern sign languages. It is the physical production mechanism of sign language, contrasting with the vocal tract used in spoken languages.

Before we explore the sorting quiz below, let's make sure we can distinguish between these different communication modes.

docs.title: 2. What is American Sign Language?
docs.text:
American Sign Language (ASL) is a complete, natural language that is the primary language of many Deaf people in the United States and parts of Canada.

It is important to understand what ASL is not: * It is not English on the hands. ASL has its own unique grammar, sentence structure, rules, and vocabulary that are completely separate from English. * It is not universal. Deaf people in different countries use different sign languages. For example, British Sign Language (BSL) and French Sign Language (LSF) are entirely different languages from ASL. * It is not just simple gestures. Gestures are informal body movements we use to emphasize speech. ASL signs are formal, structured vocabulary words with precise rules.

As a natural language, ASL has evolved over hundreds of years. It features a rich literature, including poetry, storytelling, and theatrical performances, all designed for visual expression.

docs.title: 3. The Deaf Community and Deaf Culture
docs.text: To learn ASL is to learn about the people who speak it. The language and its speakers are deeply intertwined.

docs.title: The Deaf Community
docs.text:
The Deaf Community is a diverse group of individuals who share a common linguistic and cultural bond. This community is not defined simply by a medical diagnosis of hearing loss. Instead, it is a social group that includes: * Deaf individuals who use ASL to communicate. * Hard-of-hearing individuals who identify with the community. * Hearing family members, friends, interpreters, and educators who participate in Deaf culture.

Within the community, the word "Deaf" is spelled with a capital "D" when referring to the cultural and social group (Deaf Culture), and with a lowercase "d" when referring to the physiological condition of not hearing (deafness).

docs.title: Deaf Culture
docs.text:
Deaf Culture consists of the unique values, social beliefs, traditions, and artistic expressions shared by the Deaf community. Some core values of Deaf Culture include: * Visual Alert Systems: Using flashing lights for doorbells, smoke detectors, and baby monitors instead of sound alarms. * Collectivism: A strong sense of group loyalty, community support, and shared history. * Directness: Clear, honest, and direct communication is highly valued. * Storytelling: Visual storytelling and sign play are celebrated traditions.

!!! mascot-thinking "For Reflection" { class="mascot-admonition-img" } Why do you think the Deaf community prefers to define itself by culture and language rather than by hearing loss? Think about how spoken languages (like Spanish or French) define distinct cultural groups.

docs.title: 4. The Five Parameters of ASL
docs.text:
Just like spoken words are made of individual sounds (phonemes), ASL signs are built from five distinct physical components called parameters. If you change even one parameter, you change the entire meaning of the sign—or turn it into a nonsense gesture.

The five parameters of ASL are: 1. Handshape: The configuration of your hand (e.g., flat, fist, index finger pointed). 2. Palm Orientation: The direction your palm faces (e.g., forward, backward, left, right). 3. Location: The physical spot on or near your body where the sign is made. 4. Movement: The action or path your hands take (e.g., straight line, circle, wiggling, tapping). 5. Facial Expression (Non-Manual Signals): Grammatical facial movements and body shifts.

Let's study these parameters in detail.

Parameter Key Concept Examples in Action Handshape The shape of the hand(s). Using a flat "B" hand vs. an index "1" hand. Palm Orientation The direction the palm faces. Palm facing inward toward you vs. outward toward the receiver. Location Where the sign is physically anchored. Making a sign on your forehead vs. your chin or in neutral space. Movement The path, speed, or repetition of the hands. Moving hands in a circular path vs. a sharp downward stroke. Facial Expression Non-manual signals that convey grammar. Raising eyebrows for a question vs. furrowing them.

Before we look at the interactive explorer below, let's review how these parameters serve as the physical building blocks of ASL.

docs.title: 5. Deconstructing the Parameters
docs.text: Let's examine how each of the five parameters contributes to the structure and meaning of ASL signs.

docs.title: Handshape
docs.text:
The Handshape is the shape your hand makes. Many ASL handshapes are based on the letters of the fingerspelled alphabet or numbers (which we will learn in Chapter 2).

For example, compare the signs for MY and I/ME: * To sign MY, you use a flat, open handshape (often called the "B" handshape) pressed against your chest. * To sign I/ME, you use an index finger handshape (the "1" handshape) pointing to your chest. The only difference between these two signs is the shape of your hand.

docs.title: Palm Orientation
docs.text:
Palm Orientation refers to which way your palm is facing. Your palm can face inward (toward yourself), outward (toward the receiver), up, down, left, or right.

For example, look at the signs for CLEAN and PAPER: * For both signs, you place your dominant hand flat on top of your non-dominant hand. * For CLEAN, your palm slides smoothly across. * For PAPER, the palms brush against each other in a repeating backward motion. Changing palm orientation changes the meaning entirely!

!!! mascot-tip "Fingerspelling Tip" { class="mascot-admonition-img" } When fingerspelling or signing numbers, keep your palm facing outward toward the person you are communicating with. Turning your palm inward makes it hard for others to read your signs!

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
Location is the physical position of the sign. Signs can be made on the forehead, face, chin, neck, shoulders, chest, or in the open space in front of your body (called neutral space).

For example, look at the gender signs in ASL: * Signs for male family members are made near the forehead (temple area). * Signs for female family members are made near the chin (jawline area). * FATHER is signed by tapping the thumb of an open "5" hand on the forehead. * MOTHER is signed by tapping the thumb of an open "5" hand on the chin. Everything about these signs is identical except for their location!

docs.title: Movement
docs.text:
Movement is the action of your hands. Signs can move in straight lines, arcs, circles, wiggles, waves, or repeating taps. Movement can be fast or slow, showing intensity or duration.

For example, look at nouns and verbs: * In ASL, nouns (objects) often have a double, smaller movement. * Verbs (actions) often have a single, larger movement. * CHAIR (noun) is signed with two quick, small downward taps of the fingers. * SIT (verb) is signed with a single, larger downward movement.

docs.title: Facial Expression (Non-Manual Signals)
docs.text:
Facial Expression, also called Non-Manual Signals (NMS), refers to movements of your face and body that accompany your signs. This is not just decoration—it is the literal grammar of ASL!

Facial expressions carry meaning: * Yes/No Questions: Raise your eyebrows and tilt your head forward. * WH-Questions (Who, What, When, Where, Why): Furrow (lower) your eyebrows and tilt your head forward. * Negation (saying "no" or "not"): Shake your head from side to side while signing.

Without facial expressions, your signing is like speaking in a flat, expressionless computer voice!

!!! mascot-warning "Common Mistake" { class="mascot-admonition-img" } Don't look down at your hands while signing! Keep your eyes on the face of the person you are communicating with, and look them in the eyes. In Deaf culture, eye contact is crucial for clear communication.

docs.title: 6. How Parameter Shifts Change Meaning
docs.text:
Because ASL signs are constructed from these parameters, changing just one parameter alters the sign's meaning. Linguists call this a parameter shift. It is the ASL equivalent of changing a single sound in a spoken word (like changing the "c" in "cat" to "h" to make "hat").

Before we use the comparison tool below, let's review how a shift in a single parameter (Location or Palm Orientation) completely alters the vocabulary word.

docs.text:
To tie these concepts together, it is helpful to look at how they relate to one another. American Sign Language sits inside Manual Communication and Visual Communication, built on the foundation of the 5 parameters.

docs.title: 8. Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text: Visual languages are just as rich and structured as spoken languages. By understanding how ASL is constructed, you are ready to begin fingerspelling, signing numbers, and building conversations.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Language Mode: ASL is a visual-gestural language, not a spoken one. It uses manual production (hands, body) and visual reception (eyes).
  • ASL Identity: ASL has its own grammar and structure completely separate from English.
  • The Deaf Community: Defined culturally and linguistically (Deaf with a capital "D"), sharing unique cultural values.
  • The 5 Parameters: Handshape, Palm Orientation, Location, Movement, and Facial Expression are the contrastive units of any sign.
  • Facial Grammar: Non-manual signals (like raising or lowering eyebrows) carry the actual grammar and sentence structure of ASL.

!!! mascot-encourage "Keep Practicing!" { class="mascot-admonition-img" } Learning a visual language is a new workout for your brain and your hands! If your fingers feel a little stiff or your face feels tired from practicing expressions, that's completely normal. Your muscle memory will build up quickly with practice!

!!! mascot-celebration "Congratulations on Chapter 1!" { class="mascot-admonition-img" } You've completed Chapter 1 and mastered the foundations of American Sign Language! You now understand the five parameters and the rich culture behind the language. I'm so proud of your progress—let's keep the momentum going in Chapter 2!

docs.title: Learning Graph for Introduction to American Sign Language
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: ASL Hand Viewer
docs.text: An interactive 3D hand visualization tool for exploring American Sign Language hand positions using three.js.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• 3D Hand Model: Procedurally generated hand with realistic proportions
  • Preset ASL Poses: Quick access to common hand shapes including ASL letters A, B, C and "I Love You"
  • Individual Finger Control: Fine-tune each finger's curl position with sliders
  • Orbit Controls: Rotate, pan, and zoom to view the hand from any angle
  • Joint Visualization: Toggle visibility of joint markers for educational purposes
  • Mirror Mode: Switch between right and left hand views

docs.title: Included Poses
docs.text: Pose Description Open Hand All fingers extended Fist All fingers fully curled Point Index finger extended, others curled ASL 'A' Fist with thumb alongside ASL 'B' Flat hand with thumb tucked ASL 'C' Curved hand forming C shape I Love You Thumb, index, and pinky extended

docs.title: Technical Details
docs.text:
This visualization is built with:

  • Three.js (r128) - 3D rendering library
  • OrbitControls - Camera manipulation
  • Procedural geometry - Hand built from cylinders and spheres

docs.title: Hand Model Structure
docs.text: The hand model uses a hierarchical bone structure: - Palm (base) - Each finger has 3-4 segments (metacarpal, proximal, middle, distal) - Joints between segments allow rotation for curling motion - Thumb has special positioning and rotation for realistic movement
